comedic_beats.description: Husband flatly asks what she told his mom; wife answers 'That we're still figuring it out' in a flat, unbothered tone while continuing to dry a plate.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The wife delivers the line without breaking her dish-drying rhythm or changing her droopy, half-lidded expression seen in scene-1's close-up, playing the white lie as mundane housework rather than a confession.

comedic_beats.description: The husband contradicts the lie by stating the plain fact: 'We figured it out three years ago,' revealing the couple has privately and permanently decided against kids while publicly stringing the mother along.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The 0.64s pause beforehand (4.93-5.57 in silence_pauses.json) sets up the correction like a punchline turn, and the specific 'three years ago' detail (versus a vague 'we decided') makes the gap between the public excuse and the settled private truth land as a joke about long-married-couple secrecy.

comedic_beats.description: Wife's closing button line 'She doesn't need to know that' is followed by a 1.2-second silent hold on the characters' tired faces before the scene cuts.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The 1.198s pause (the longest gap in silence_pauses.json) is held on the husband's exhausted, glasses-slid-down expression from scene-2, letting the audience sit in the casual moral shrug instead of rushing to the next scene, which is what sells the resignation as funny rather than sad.

comedic_beats.description: Overall scenario of a couple who feel worn down and are low-key withholding truth from an in-law about kids, rendered with sagging, low-energy 'low battery' facial rigging (droopy eyes, long weary noses, hunched posture).
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The character design itself (permanently tired eyes, sagging brows visible in both scene-1 and scene-2 keyframes) primes the joke before any dialogue lands, so viewers recognize 'exhausted married couple dodging a nosy parent' as a lived-in type rather than a one-off gag.

overall_comedic_style_notes: The humor here is a two-hander built entirely on dry, matter-of-fact line readings from visibly weary stop-motion characters (part of a 'Low Battery People' series per the scene-3 title card) -- there is no slapstick or visual sight gag, just a domestic white lie exposed by a flat correction, capped with a long silent reaction hold instead of a punchline sting. Comedy comes from understatement: characters keep doing chores (drying dishes, washing up) through the reveal, refusing to react big, which reads as ironic deadpan rather than farce.
